'''Olrat''' is an extinct [[Oceanic language]] of [[Gaua|Gaua island]], in northern [[Vanuatu]]. It became extinct in 2009 with the death of its last speaker, Maten Womal.<ref name="pangloss">[[#pangloss|François (2022)]].</ref>

==Name==
The name ''Olrat'' (spelled natively as ''Ōlrat'' {{IPA|olr|ʊlrat|}}) is an endonym. [[Robert Henry Codrington|Robert Codrington]] mentions a place south of Lakon village under the [[Mota language|Mota]] name ''Ulrata''.<ref>See [https://archive.org/details/melanesianlangua00codruoft/page/378/mode/1up page 378] of: {{cite book
|last=Codrington
|first=R. H.
|author-link=Robert Henry Codrington
|year=1885
|title = The Melanesian Languages
|volume = 47
|pages = 25–60
|publisher = Clarendon Press
|place = Oxford
|url= https://archive.org/details/melanesianlangua00codruoft
|ref=RHC
}}</ref> A few decades later, [[Sidney Herbert Ray|Sidney Ray]] mentions the language briefly in 1926 under the name Ulrata ‒ but provides no linguistic information.<ref>See [https://books.google.com/books?id=IeE8AAAAIAAJ&q=%22Volow%22&pg=PA428 page 428] of: {{cite book |title=A Comparative Study of the Melanesian Island Languages |last=Ray |first=Sidney Herbert |authorlink=Sidney Herbert Ray |year=1926 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge |isbn=9781107682023 |pages=xvi+598 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=h9tkAwAAQBAJ |accessdate= |ref=Ray}}.</ref>

==Speakers==
[[File:Alex-Maten-Gaua-2003.jpg|thumb|250px|upright|{{center|A. François with †Maten Womal, the last storyteller of Olrat <small>([[Gaua]], [[Vanuatu]], 2003)</small>}}]]

In 2003, only three speakers of Olrat remained, who lived on the middle-west coast of Gaua.<ref name="sociolg" /><ref>[https://marama.huma-num.fr/AF-field.htm List of Banks islands languages].</ref> Their community had left their inland hamlet of Olrat in the first half of the 20th century, and merged into the larger village of Jōlap where [[Lakon language|Lakon]] is dominant.<ref name="sociolg">{{Harvcoltxt|François|2012}}.</ref><ref name="pangloss" />

[[Alexandre François (linguist)|Alexandre François]] identifies Olrat as a distinct language from its immediate neighbor [[Lakon language|Lakon]], on phonological,<ref>{{Harvcoltxt|François|2005}}</ref> grammatical,<ref>{{Harvcoltxt|François|2007}}</ref> and lexical<ref>{{Harvcoltxt|François|2011}}</ref> grounds.
==Phonology==
Olrat has 14 [[phoneme|phonemic]] vowels. These include 7 short /i ɪ ɛ a ɔ ʊ u/ and 7 long vowels /iː ɪː ɛː aː ɔː ʊː uː/.<ref>{{Harvcoltxt|François|2005|p=445}}, {{Harvcoltxt|François|2011|p=194}}.</ref><ref name="pangloss" />

Historically, the phonologization of vowel length originates in the [[compensatory lengthening]] of short vowels when the [[voiced velar fricative]] {{IPA|/ɣ/}} was lost syllable-finally.<ref>{{Harvcoltxt|François|2005|p=461}}.</ref>

==Grammar==
The system of [[personal pronoun]]s in Olrat contrasts [[clusivity]], and distinguishes four [[Grammatical number|numbers]] (singular, [[Dual number|dual]], [[Trial number|trial]], plural).<ref>[[#pronouns|François (2016)]].</ref>

Spatial reference in Olrat is based on a system of geocentric ([[Linguistic frame of reference#Absolute frame of reference|absolute]]) directionals, which is typical of [[Oceanic languages]].<ref>[[#updown|François (2015)]].</ref>
